Survey-weighted concentration index

Source: R/survey_concentration_index.R
survey_concentration_index.Rd

Computes the concentration index of a health variable across a socioeconomic ranking (for example a wealth score), with design-based standard errors, confidence intervals and p-values that account for stratification and clustering. The standard, generalized, Erreygers and Wagstaff indices are available.

Usage

survey_concentration_index(
  design,
  outcome,
  wealth,
  conf.level = 0.95,
  type = c("CI", "generalized", "erreygers", "wagstaff"),
  bounds = NULL,
  by = NULL
)

Arguments

design

A survey design object (survey or srvyr).

outcome

Unquoted name of the health variable.

wealth

Unquoted name of the ranking variable.

conf.level

Confidence level.

type

One of "CI" (default), "generalized", "erreygers", "wagstaff".

bounds

Numeric vector c(a, b) of the outcome's bounds, needed for "erreygers" and "wagstaff". Defaults to c(0, 1) when the outcome is binary.

by

Optional character vector of grouping columns; ranks are computed within each group.

Value

A tibble of class surveyncd_ci with any by columns, Concentration_Index, Standard_Error, Lower_CI, Upper_CI, p_value, Outcome_Mean, n and Type.

Details

The standard concentration index is $$C = \frac{2}{\mu} \mathrm{cov}_w(y_i, R_i),$$ where \(\mu\) is the weighted mean of \(y\) and \(R_i\) the weighted fractional rank: the mid-point of each respondent's interval of the cumulative weight distribution (Lerman and Yitzhaki 1989). Respondents tied on the ranking variable share the mid-point of their tied group's interval, so results do not depend on the order of the data.

Each index is the slope \(\beta\) of the "convenient regression" of Kakwani, Wagstaff and van Doorslaer (1997), \(2\sigma_R^2 \, h(y_i) = \alpha + \beta R_i + \varepsilon_i\), fitted with survey::svyglm() so that its standard error is design-based. With bounds \(a \le y \le b\) (O'Donnell et al. 2016):

  • "CI" (standard): \(h(y) = y/\mu\).

  • "generalized": \(h(y) = y\), giving \(\mu C\).

  • "erreygers": \(h(y) = 4y/(b - a)\), giving \(4\mu C/(b-a)\) (Erreygers 2009).

  • "wagstaff": \(h(y) = (b - a)y/((b - \mu)(\mu - a))\), giving \((b-a)\mu C/((b-\mu)(\mu-a))\); for binary outcomes \(C/(1-\mu)\) (Wagstaff 2005).

For bounded outcomes such as binary indicators the Erreygers or Wagstaff index is usually preferred. The standard error treats the ranks and \(\mu\) as fixed.

References

Kakwani, N., Wagstaff, A., & van Doorslaer, E. (1997). Socioeconomic inequalities in health: Measurement, computation, and statistical inference. Journal of Econometrics, 77(1), 87-103. doi:10.1016/S0304-4076(96)01807-6

Erreygers, G. (2009). Correcting the concentration index. Journal of Health Economics, 28(2), 504-515. doi:10.1016/j.jhealeco.2008.02.003

Wagstaff, A. (2005). The bounds of the concentration index when the variable of interest is binary, with an application to immunization inequality. Health Economics, 14(4), 429-432. doi:10.1002/hec.953

O'Donnell, O., O'Neill, S., Van Ourti, T., & Walsh, B. (2016). conindex: Estimation of concentration indices. The Stata Journal, 16(1), 112-138. doi:10.1177/1536867X1601600112

Examples

set.seed(42)
n <- 50
df <- data.frame(
  wealth  = rnorm(n, 50, 15),
  outcome = pmax(0, 0.3 * rnorm(n, 50, 15) + rnorm(n, 0, 5)),
  sick    = rbinom(n, 1, 0.3),
  wt      = sample(1:5, n, replace = TRUE)
)
design <- survey::svydesign(ids = ~1, weights = ~wt, data = df)
survey_concentration_index(design, outcome = outcome, wealth = wealth)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 8
#>   Concentration_Index Standard_Error Lower_CI Upper_CI p_value Outcome_Mean
#>                 <dbl>          <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1             -0.0242         0.0370  -0.0967   0.0483   0.513         15.1
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: n <int>, Type <chr>
survey_concentration_index(design, outcome = sick, wealth = wealth,
                           type = "erreygers")
#> # A tibble: 1 × 8
#>   Concentration_Index Standard_Error Lower_CI Upper_CI p_value Outcome_Mean
#>                 <dbl>          <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1             -0.0101          0.188   -0.379    0.359   0.957        0.336
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: n <int>, Type <chr>
